extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, and judges (those drafting or construing patent specifications and claims)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to draft and construe patent specifications and claims so they (a) properly describe the invention, (b) avoid claiming abstract principles, and (c) set an appropriate scope that enables others and supports enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe the improvement by showing parts and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to describe the improvement, by showing the parts of which it consists, and the effects which it produces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must disclose the components and the results produced so the invention is ascertainable; applied throughout the discussion (e.g., in chemical and mechanical inventions). Example: the patent should state what is added to iron and the effect (prevention of 'cold short').

rubrics_metrics.name: For machines: fully explain the principle and several modes of application
rubrics_metrics.description: "And in case of any machine, he (the patentee) shall fully explain the principle and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle ... and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination, which he claims as his own invention or discovery."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory requirement: explain the characteristic principle of the machine, the modes of applying it (including variations the patentee intends to cover), and point out the exact parts or combination claimed. The patentee should state the 'character by which it may be distinguished from other inventions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the 'principle' as the peculiar structure and mode of operation
rubrics_metrics.description: By the principle of a machine ... is to be understood the peculiar structure and mode of operation of such machine; or, as the statute itself explains it, the character by which it may be distinguished from other inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking a 'principle' in a specification, tie it to a concrete structure and mode of operation so the claim reads as an application embodied in matter rather than an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point out all modes of application claimed, but minute variations need not be described in detail
rubrics_metrics.description: He is to state not only the peculiar device or construction which he deems the best ... but also all the other modes of producing the same effect, which he means to claim as being substantially applications of the same principle. In doing this, it is not necessary for him to enter into a minute description of the mode of producing those variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate variations of application you intend to cover; you need not detail every minor structural variation, but you should indicate what sorts of variations are claimed beyond the preferred embodiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim mere abstract principles or laws of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent cannot be taken out solely for an abstract philosophical principle ... The mere discovery of such a principle is not an invention, in the patent law sense of the term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject is a scientific principle or law of nature, the specification must show its practical application to a special purpose by incorporation with matter so as to produce a practical result. Without that application, the claim is void. Cases cited: Barrett v. Hall; Househill Co. v. Neilson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe some practical mode of carrying the principle into effect
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential that the specification should describe some practical mode of carrying the principle into effect; and then the subject-matter will be patentable, because it will be, not the principle itself, but the mode of carrying it into effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide at least one working embodiment or mechanical contrivance that applies the principle to a specified result so the invention is enabling and patentable; otherwise the claim risks being declared an abstract principle (Wyeth v. Stone example).

rubrics_metrics.name: General claims may cover all forms of apparatus applying the same principle to a specified result
rubrics_metrics.description: If you suggest and invent how [a principle] may be applied to a practical result by mechanical contrivance and apparatus, and show that you are aware that no particular sort or modification or form of the apparatus is essential, then you may take your patent for the mode of carrying the principle into effect ... and you are not under the necessity of describing and confining yourself to one form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broad claim directed to the application of a principle for a specified beneficial result can lawfully embrace multiple apparatus forms (Neilson hot-blast example). The generality of the claim is not per se fatal; it can be a merit, not an objection, provided the patentee has disclosed a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of means producing same beneficial effect can still infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: A variation of the means and machinery, if it produces the same beneficial effect, that is, is the same application of the same principle, does not show that the party making such variation has not infringed the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On infringement, courts/juries assess whether a different mode is a colorable imitation of the patented mode; different shapes or apparatus that embody the same application of the principle may be infringing (jury determines factual similarity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims of entire/absolute discovery must account for prior use; qualify as improvement if needed
rubrics_metrics.description: So far, therefore, the application of lime is, in terms claimed as an improvement, and nothing is said of any previous use, of which the use proposed is averred to be an improvement; it is, therefore, in substance, a claim of entire and original discovery ... The recital should have stated, supposing a previous use to be proved in the case, that, 'whereas lime has been in part, but improperly, made use of, &c.' and then a different mode of application and use should have been suggested as the improvement claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft recitals and claims to acknowledge prior uses and frame the invention as an improvement where appropriate; claiming sweeping 'discovery' of an effect when prior use exists can render the patent void.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a combination is claimed, the patent is for the whole combination only
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a combination of three things cannot at the same time be a patent for a combination of any two of them. If the subject-matter is the combination of any given number of things ... no portion of the combination less than the whole can be considered at the same time as being also the subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claiming a combination, be aware that subsets of the combination are not automatically covered as separate claims; if parts are not new, consider whether the claim can be sustained as a combination. Construction and validity depend on factual specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit nothing material and avoid misleading the public
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule ... requires the patentee so to describe his invention as to enable the public to know what his claim is, it of course imposes upon him the duty of not misleading the public, either by concealing anything material to the invention, or by adding any-
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conceal material elements, and avoid misleading statements or unnecessary verbiage that obscures what is claimed. Failure to disclose essential features is a serious defect; omission of only contributory non-essential details is less likely fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement: specification must enable others to apply the principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must give [the discovery] a practical application to some useful purpose ... and his specification must show the application of the principle to such a special purpose, by its incorporation with matter in such a way as to be in a condition to produce a practical result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement requires enough detail for a person skilled in the art to carry the invention into practice and use the claimed principle for the stated purpose; even if best modes are not fully worked out, showing practical application suffices (Watt example).
